identification.summary: CrowdStrike published its profile of PLA Navy-linked 'Anchor Panda' on 2013-03-22. It said it had tracked the adversary for about a year, targeting civilian and military maritime operations in green/brown water regions, mainly the area of operations of the PLA Navy South Sea Fleet [S1]. Beyond maritime targets it said the actor heavily targeted Western companies in the US, Germany, Sweden, the UK and Australia, plus other countries involved in maritime satellite systems, aerospace and defense contracting [S1]. CFR's cyber operations tracker lists the activity as espionage with China as suspected sponsor [S2].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike said in March 2013 that it had tracked the actor for roughly the previous year (about 2012) [S1].
identification.notes: Vendor naming varies by source. This record's aliases (ALUMINUM, QAZTeam, ANCHOR PANDA) came from MISP Galaxy; a search-result summary of the Malpedia APT14 page also lists Anchor Panda, ALUMINUM and QAZTeam under APT14. An earlier note that Malpedia places these under APT15 was not supported by this check and was removed. Do not merge activity across APT14/APT15 without a primary report. No Microsoft Typhoon/Storm name was confirmed for this actor. No MITRE group ID is recorded.

attribution.sponsor: CrowdStrike's own title calls the actor 'PLA Navy Anchor Panda' and ties its focus to the PLA Navy South Sea Fleet area of operations [S1]. CFR lists China as suspected state sponsor [S2].
attribution.confidence: No confidence level is stated in the sources I could read. CFR labels the sponsor as 'suspected' [S2]. This is vendor-level attribution; no government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: CrowdStrike cites target selection aligned with PLA Navy South Sea Fleet interests; its detailed technical basis was withheld in the post [S1].

objectives: Collection of maritime, satellite, aerospace and defense-contractor information and political/diplomatic intelligence, inferred by CrowdStrike from victim selection around the South Sea Fleet area and space-related industries [S1].

regions: South Sea Fleet area of operations (green/brown water) [S1]
United States, Germany, Sweden, United Kingdom, Australia [S1]
targeting.notes: Targeting described by CrowdStrike in 2013 [S1]. No later targeting reporting was found.

capabilities.summary: CrowdStrike's post said it would withhold most technical detail but included detection signatures; secondary summaries say these covered Adobe Gh0st and Poison Ivy beacons, and one secondary source also mentions Torn RAT and spear-phishing (not verified against the primary text) [S1].

campaigns.name: CrowdStrike 'Who is Anchor Panda' disclosure
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike publicly profiled the actor, describing about a year of tracked maritime, satellite, aerospace and defense-contractor targeting across several Western countries and the South China Sea region.

diamond.adversary: Suspected PRC actor with apparent PLA Navy tasking alignment, per CrowdStrike [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Remote access tools (Poison Ivy, Gh0st variants) per signatures in the CrowdStrike post, as summarized by secondary sources [S1].
diamond.victim: Maritime operators, satellite/aerospace firms, defense contractors, embassies, intelligence services and space-program governments [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Naval and maritime interests in the South China Sea region and space-related technology acquisition [S1].
diamond.technology: Maritime satellite systems and aerospace/defense industrial networks [S1].

gaps: No reporting after March 2013 was found; current activity status is unknown.
Could not open the primary CrowdStrike post (host unreachable from tooling); capability details rely on search-result summaries of it.
No Microsoft actor name, MITRE group, malware list, infrastructure, or CVEs confirmed.
Mandiant APT-groups page listed in the record was not reviewed.
Alias mapping (APT14 vs APT15) not verified against a primary report; Malpedia, MISP Galaxy and Red Sky Alliance pages were seen only as search results and are not cited as sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Maritime satellite ground and communications nodes, shipping and port-related networks, and aerospace/defense contractor networks supporting naval and space programs are candidate key terrain [S1]. STEP 2: The actor aligns with the PLA Navy South Sea Fleet area of operations, so collection interest likely rises around South China Sea activity [S1]. STEP 3: Template is RAT-based intrusion (Gh0st/Poison Ivy-type per secondary summaries) against contractors and maritime operators [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against maritime, satellite and defense-industrial targets. MDCOA is use of access to defense contractors or satellite providers to learn US/allied maritime posture during a crisis. Candidate indicators: Poison Ivy/Gh0st-style beacons from maritime or satellite-sector hosts. Evidence is dated 2013 and thin.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat as low-confidence legacy reporting; confirm current activity before tasking. (2) Authorities: contractor and commercial maritime/satellite networks fall outside DoDIN; coordinate through DC3/DIB CS and sector partners. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize protection of satellite communications and maritime logistics dependencies in the Indo-Pacific. (4) Coordination: confirm actor naming with intelligence partners before sharing indicators.

provenance.importedSummary: PLA Navy Anchor Panda is an adversary that CrowdStrike has tracked extensively over the last year targeting both civilian and military maritime operations in the green/brown water regions primarily in the area of operations of the South Sea Fleet of the PLA Navy. In addition to maritime operations in this region, Anchor Panda also heavily targeted western companies in the US, Germany, Sweden, the UK, and Australia, and other countries involved in maritime satellite systems, aerospace companies, and defense contractors. Not surprisingly, embassies and diplomatic missions in the region, foreign intelligence services, and foreign governments with space programs were also targeted.
